Good afternoon, private banking. Rachel Tan speaking. How may I help you?

Hello Rachel, Adrian Lim here. Calling about arranging a disposal from my existing portfolio. Finally got a quiet stretch at the office, so I thought better call rather than start another email chain. Have you got time to speak? I don't need to rush off immediately today lah.

Hello, Adrian. Yes, I have time to speak with you. We can take the conversation at a comfortable pace. Are you somewhere you can speak privately, or would you prefer a moment to settle before we begin?

I'm in my own room, door closed already. The warehouse side is still busy, but they know not to keep coming in unless something really needs me. Let me put my notebook in front of me. My NRIC is S four eight five two three zero seven L.

I have your NRIC as S four one five two three zero seven L. Is that correct?

No, you heard it wrongly. My NRIC is S four eight five two three zero seven L. My date of birth is 28 April 1972. The connection sounded a bit muffled just now leh. I've taken you off the speaker, should be clearer this way.

Thank you for correcting me, and I apologise for the error. Your voice is clearer now. Before we get into the rest of the conversation, I want to set out the objective recorded for this discussion. Your investment objective is to reduce exposure to market fluctuations and release liquidity from your existing investments for greater personal financial flexibility. I've noted that as your objective.

Let me just shift away from the door ah. Someone outside is moving a trolley and the wheels are making a terrible noise. This office used to feel very quiet, then we changed the layout and suddenly every sound comes through. All right, I'm settled now.

There is no need to hurry. You mentioned that you finally have some uninterrupted time. Has the business been keeping you particularly occupied, or have you been able to pass more of the routine work to your colleagues?

Still quite occupied lor, but I'm trying to change that. In a family business, everyone gets used to asking the same person. Even when somebody else can answer, they come to me out of habit. I step out to get a drink, come back, and got a small queue outside my room already.

That sounds as though the informal arrangements have lasted longer than the formal job descriptions. When you try to step back, is the difficulty that people are unsure who is responsible, or that they simply feel more comfortable asking you?

More the comfort part lah. The staff know their jobs. Sometimes they already have the answer but want me to say it before they send anything out. I'm trying not to become the final stop for every small matter. Otherwise I say I'm delegating, but actually nothing changes.

Has the team had a chance to work without you being immediately available? It can be quite different when you are away from the office rather than simply behind a closed door. I am interested in whether your recent time away gave you a proper break.

That was quite revealing actually. When I travelled, they managed better than I expected. Got questions waiting when I returned, of course, but most were things they had already resolved. Then I realised some of the problem is me. I see a message and reply too quickly, so everyone keeps checking with me.

It sounds as though being away gave you a different view of how the office works. Did you enjoy the distance, or did you find yourself missing the daily activity? People who have been closely involved for a long time sometimes describe both feelings at once.

Both, correct. At first my hand kept reaching for the phone. Quite ridiculous leh, sitting somewhere peaceful and checking whether somebody received a delivery note. After a while I stopped looking so often. Nothing dramatic happened. The business still opened, the customers still called, and everyone carried on without my running commentary.

Were you able to keep that separation when you came back, or did the office routine draw you straight in again?

First morning back, straight into the usual pattern already. Somebody put a stack of papers on my chair and I automatically started sorting them. Then I caught myself. Now I ask who is actually handling the matter before I touch anything. Not because I don't want to help lah, but I don't want to take the work back without noticing.

That is a meaningful distinction. From our side, when we contact you about routine banking administration, would you still prefer that we contact you directly? I would not want your work on delegation within the business to be mistaken for a change in how you want your personal banking handled.

Personal banking, contact me directly please. The office team don't need to be in the middle of that. Business responsibilities can move around, but my personal correspondence I still want to see myself. Just keep the messages straightforward ah. If an email looks like a whole project, I tend to leave it until the evening.

We can keep that distinction clear in our conversation. A concise message that identifies the purpose is different from copying you into a long exchange. When you do need to discuss something, is calling generally easier than working through a series of written replies?

Much easier. Email sometimes becomes a strange game. I answer the main question, then somebody replies about a side point, then the original question disappears under all the quotations. On the phone I can say what I actually mean. Not saying don't write anything lah; just don't make me dig through a long thread to find the part meant for me.

A conversation can be useful for establishing the context, with written communication kept focused on its purpose. Is the difficulty mainly the volume of email, or do you also find that the tone can be misread when people are trying to be brief?

The tone also got problem sometimes. I type a short answer because I'm between meetings, then people think I'm annoyed. My family tease me about it. Apparently a full stop from me looks very stern. I thought proper punctuation was supposed to help, but now even punctuation got personality already.

That does seem to happen in quick messages. At least on a call there is room to hear when someone is smiling. I will keep my questions direct, and you are welcome to stop me if something I say does not match what you intended.

That suits me. If I interrupt, not trying to be rude ah. Sometimes easier to catch something straight away than wait until the whole explanation is finished. At work I tell the staff the same thing. Better a brief interruption than everybody politely walking in different directions.

You corrected the earlier readback promptly, which was helpful. Apart from the business, have you managed to keep any time free for yourself since returning from your trip? You sounded pleased that the quieter surroundings had given you a break from the usual routine.

Yes, the trip was good. Nothing very ambitious lah. We stayed somewhere with a garden and a quiet place to sit outside. No pressure to chase attractions from morning until night. These days I enjoy waking up without somebody announcing that we must leave immediately or miss something.

Was that a deliberate change from the way you used to travel, or have quieter places always appealed to you?

Last time I was more concerned about making the trip worthwhile. Reach somewhere, must see everything, otherwise feel wasted. Now I come home and ask myself whether I actually rested. Walking slowly, finding somewhere pleasant for lunch, sitting with a book—like that also quite enjoyable what. No need every day to become a production.

Did the rest of the family enjoy that pace as well? It can be difficult to choose a holiday style when people want different things from the same trip.

Some prefer more activity, sure. But this time we didn't insist on doing everything together. If somebody wanted to go out, they went. If I wanted to stay in the garden, nobody made a speech about it. Much more relaxed lor. Meeting again for a meal gave us enough to talk about.

That sounds companionable without requiring everyone to follow the same schedule. Was there anything about the place that you particularly enjoyed and would look for again?

The quiet in the morning. Not silent until uncomfortable, just normal sounds outside instead of traffic and people dragging suitcases along a corridor. Got an old bench under some trees. I sat there with my coffee and didn't feel I had to photograph it or tell anybody. That part stayed with me more than the sightseeing.

It is often a very ordinary detail that makes a place memorable. Would you go back, or do you prefer to find somewhere different rather than repeat a trip?

I don't mind going back lah. People always ask why return when there are so many places to see. But if I enjoyed somewhere, why must I turn the next holiday into research? Familiar also has its advantages. You know where to get breakfast and which path is pleasant for a walk. Less arranging, more actual holiday.

I can see why that would appeal when so much of your working life involves arranging things for other people. Did you manage to leave the itinerary fairly open, or were there still family plans to coordinate?

Fairly open, thankfully. The real coordination is happening now, back home. We're trying to arrange a family gathering and suddenly everyone's calendar looks more complicated than a delivery schedule. Got people working late, people travelling, people waiting to hear about something else. Nobody wants to be difficult, but getting a clear answer takes effort.

Are you the person everyone expects to bring those arrangements together as well?

Usually I become that person without applying for the job. Someone asks whether we should meet, I reply, then somehow I'm responsible for the restaurant and all the reminders already. This time I'm trying to let somebody else coordinate. But then I catch myself asking whether they have heard back from everyone. A bit hopeless hor.

It can be difficult to change a familiar family role. Do you enjoy the gathering once the arrangements are settled, or does the organising make it feel like another responsibility?

Once everyone arrives, I enjoy it very much. The organising is the tiring part, not the people. Sitting around after the food, hearing what everyone has been doing—that's nice. At the office we mostly talk about work. At a family meal got other stories, and you remember there is life outside the business.

Does work tend to follow you into those gatherings, or are people able to leave it aside?

It tries to follow us in lah. Somebody will mention a customer or ask about something they saw at the office. Then another person complains that we've brought the meeting room to dinner. Usually that stops it. I don't mind a passing comment, but I don't want the whole evening to become a review of unfinished work.

That seems a fair distinction. With both family and business overlapping, a separate conversation can easily become part of the working day. Do the younger family members take an interest in the business, or do they prefer to talk about entirely different things?

A mixture. Some are interested, some politely escape the moment we start. Can't blame them lah. When I was younger, I also didn't enjoy hearing adults discuss stock deliveries over dinner. Now I hear myself doing it and think, aiyoh, I've become the person I used to avoid sitting beside.

At least you can recognise it and laugh about it. Are you hoping that passing on routine work will make it easier to be present at those gatherings without carrying the office with you?

That's part of the everyday change I'm trying to make. Not some grand retirement announcement ah. I still enjoy being involved, especially talking to people we have known for a long time. I just don't need to be the person who knows where every document has gone. Other people can own their work properly.

There is a difference between staying involved and being continually available. From a practical contact perspective, would an unexpected call during the working day usually reach you, or is a brief message beforehand less disruptive?

A message beforehand is useful. If I'm with a supplier, I may see the phone and not be able to answer. Then I spend the rest of the meeting wondering whether the call was urgent. Just tell me what the conversation is about in ordinary language. No need to put private details into a message lah.

That is helpful. A message can identify that we would like to speak without including sensitive information. If we do reach you at an inconvenient moment, you can simply say so; there is no need to continue a conversation while other people are nearby.

Good. Sometimes I answer because I recognise the name, then realise I'm standing in the middle of the office. Not the right place for a proper discussion. Today I deliberately came into this room before calling. Even my notebook is here already, instead of being buried under somebody else's papers.

You have made the space for it. Before we return to the portfolio discussion, was there any general difficulty with receiving or finding our correspondence that you wanted to raise? I can distinguish an administrative concern from the investment conversation.

Finding things is mostly my own problem. Got too many folders with sensible names that become completely useless when I'm in a hurry. I don't need you to redesign anything. What helps is a subject line that tells me what the message is actually about, instead of something so general that everything looks the same.

A clear subject and a clear purpose are reasonable preferences. Is there an example of the sort of wording you find unhelpful, without opening any private correspondence or reading account details aloud?

Things like 'For your attention' with nothing else. Everything in my inbox is for my attention, otherwise why send it to me? Then I open it and have to work out whether somebody wants a reply or is simply letting me know something. Quite sian after a busy day, especially when the answer turns out to be that no action is needed.

It is useful to distinguish information from a request. I cannot speak for every message you receive, but I can keep that preference in mind when preparing my own correspondence. Is it generally easier for you to review written material at your desk rather than on your phone?

At the desk, definitely. On the phone the screen is small, and if I get interrupted I forget where I stopped. At my desk I can read without balancing a cup or standing beside a lift. Still, I don't want every simple question to wait until I'm back at the computer. That's why calling is helpful lor.

That gives me a clearer picture of how you use each channel. We can use a conversation for discussion without treating an ordinary message as a substitute for it. You mentioned earlier that you had your notebook ready. Would you like a quiet moment to look through your own notes before we continue?

Let me look for a moment ah. I've mixed some office reminders into the same notebook, which is exactly the sort of thing I complain about. There's a note about a missing chair here. Not relevant to you, thankfully. I remember writing it because someone borrowed the visitor's chair and never brought it back.

Take your time. I will stay on the line while you find the relevant page.

Found it already. Before we get back to that, you asked about having time outside work. Gardening has become the thing I actually make time for. Nothing impressive to show visitors, but I enjoy going outside and seeing what has changed. At least the plants don't send follow-up emails if I haven't answered.

That is quite a contrast to the office. Have you always enjoyed gardening, or did it become more interesting when you started looking for something separate from work?

Used to leave it to other people. Then I started noticing the plants properly instead of just saying the place looked nice. Now I go out intending to look around, and suddenly I'm moving a pot or clearing fallen leaves. Quite calming leh. There's something to do, but nobody is waiting for me to chair a discussion about it.

Do you prefer the practical work itself, or is it more about having somewhere quiet to spend time?

Both again. Some days I want to do something with my hands because I've spent the whole day talking. Other days I just sit there. I used to feel that sitting without a purpose was wasting time. Now I think, where got a rule that every quiet moment must produce something? The garden helps me leave that thinking behind.

Does the family share the interest, or is it mainly your own space?

They enjoy the result more than the process lah. Everyone likes to sit outside when it looks pleasant, but when there's a bag of soil to move, suddenly got urgent things indoors. I'm exaggerating a bit. They do help. Still, I don't mind having something that isn't organised as a family project.

That makes sense. Not every interest has to become a shared responsibility. Did the garden at the place where you stayed give you any ideas, or did you prefer simply enjoying it without planning changes at home?

I took some ideas back, but nothing too ambitious. I liked how they left space instead of filling every corner. At home I sometimes see an empty spot and immediately think something must go there. Then I end up with too many pots to move around. This time I came back thinking perhaps can leave some space alone.

It sounds as though the appeal was partly the absence of things competing for your attention. Was there a place at home where you could enjoy that same feeling without making a project of it?

There's a sheltered corner I like. Not a grand view, just somewhere I can hear the birds and not see the office phone. I moved a chair there and that was enough. My family laughed because I talked about improving the garden and then mostly improved where I sit. Fair comment lah.

If you actually use the space, that seems a worthwhile result. Do you find yourself spending time there before work, or is it more of an evening habit?

More often before work. Evening can disappear if something runs late. In the morning I haven't picked up all the day's noise yet. Even if I don't do anything in particular, I come back inside feeling less scattered. Then somebody asks where a file is and the ordinary day begins already.

Thank you for telling me about it. It is good to hear what fills the time away from the business, especially after you said how easily work can follow you home. We can return to the purpose of your call whenever you are ready to leave the everyday conversation there.

I'm ready to come back to it. Nice to have a proper conversation rather than just firing messages back and forth. Also gives me time to settle at the desk. When I call between other things, my head still half in the warehouse lah. Today I've actually put everything else aside.

Then let us return to your notes. I will keep the conversation focused, and if you need a pause, you can take it. There is no need to fill a silence simply because we are on the telephone.

Actually that helps. Sometimes when someone goes quiet on a call, I start talking just to check they're still there. Then I lose my own train of thought. In person you can see somebody reading. On the phone, got only silence, so I assume the connection has disappeared.

If I need to pause to look at something, I can say that I am doing so. Equally, if you are reading your notes, I will not assume that you have finished speaking. You do not need to give an answer merely to keep the conversation moving.

Good, because my handwriting needs some interpretation. When I wrote this at home it all seemed obvious. Now I can see an arrow going across the page and I'm wondering what I was connecting. Nothing technical ah, just my own way of making a tidy note look untidy.

You are welcome to organise your thoughts before speaking. I will listen to what you say on the call rather than trying to infer anything from how your notes might be arranged.

That's fair. At work I'm always telling people not to guess what an old note means, and here I am trying to guess my own. Let me put the loose papers aside. Got a clear space now. The office outside has gone quiet as well, so this is probably the best time to concentrate.

I am here and listening.

Please sell 5,000 units of Crest Emerging Markets Bond Fund using a market order. Transaction amount 5m in renminbi, please.

I have heard what you have said. Take a moment if there is anything you need to correct before we continue.

Wait wait, cancel that whole order ah. Don't execute it; I want to replace it. Instead, please sell 10,000 units of Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, transaction amount 5m in renminbi. Use a limit order with a limit price of 500 Chinese yuan; below that price, don't sell ah.

I recommend that you sell Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund.

Hmm, let me sit with that for a moment ah. I'm putting the notebook aside now so I can listen without looking back and forth. No interruption from outside anymore, thankfully.

With Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, the equity holdings can fall when stock markets decline, while the bond holdings can lose value when interest rates rise. During stressed markets, those holdings can decline together, so diversification may offer less protection than expected. You could lose some or all of the capital invested in this fund. Selling may crystallise a loss on your investment.

I'm still here. Just closing the window because someone has started working outside, and the sound is carrying straight into the room. Should be quieter now lah.

Are you willing to accept investment losses, including a loss that may be crystallised by this sale?

Yes, I'm willing to accept investment losses, including a loss from selling. I want less ongoing exposure, even if I have to take a loss.

Please confirm your final instruction: sell 10,000 units of Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, with a transaction amount of 5m in renminbi, using a limit order at a limit price of 500 Chinese yuan. Does that accurately reflect the replacement instruction you want us to execute?

Yes, I confirm that final replacement instruction exactly as you read it. Please go ahead with that order.

Thank you. Before we finish, is there any practical issue about contacting you that we have not covered? I have heard your preference for direct contact about personal banking and for a brief message if a call needs to be arranged.

Nothing else on that side. If I miss a call, don't read too much into it ah. Usually I'm away from the desk or talking to someone. I do look at messages when I get back. Better that than trying to have a private conversation with people walking past.

Of course. We can leave the general contact discussion there. I appreciate you making time to speak from somewhere private today. You have been able to deal with the conversation without trying to manage the office around it.

Yes, much better this way. Normally I think I can handle everything at once, then end up asking someone to repeat themselves. Today at least I stayed in the room. The staff also survived without checking through the door, so perhaps my little delegation exercise is working already.

I hope the rest of your afternoon remains manageable. Will you be heading back into the office activity now, or have you left yourself some space before the next conversation?

Got a bit of space. I'll finish a few ordinary things here, then go out and see what needs my attention. Not going to summon everyone for a report just because I've been behind a closed door lah. They might start avoiding me if I do that.

Then I will let you return to your afternoon. Thank you for calling, Adrian, and for the conversation. I hope you also get some time in the garden when the working day is over.

Thanks, Rachel. If the weather stays pleasant, I'll sit outside for a while. No grand gardening project today, just the chair and some quiet. That one I can manage lah. Enjoy the rest of your day. Goodbye.

Thank you, Adrian. Goodbye.

Things like 'For your attention' with nothing else. Everything in my inbox is for my attention, otherwise why send it to me? Then I open it and have to work out whether somebody wants a reply or is simply letting me know something. Quite sian after a busy day, especially when the answer turns out to be that no action is needed.

It is useful to distinguish information from a request. I cannot speak for every message you receive, but I can keep that preference in mind when preparing my own correspondence. Is it generally easier for you to review written material at your desk rather than on your phone?

At the desk, definitely. On the phone the screen is small, and if I get interrupted I forget where I stopped. At my desk I can read without balancing a cup or standing beside a lift. Still, I don't want every simple question to wait until I'm back at the computer. That's why calling is helpful lor.

That gives me a clearer picture of how you use each channel. We can use a conversation for discussion without treating an ordinary message as a substitute for it. You mentioned earlier that you had your notebook ready. Would you like a quiet moment to look through your own notes before we continue?

Let me look for a moment ah. I've mixed some office reminders into the same notebook, which is exactly the sort of thing I complain about. There's a note about a missing chair here. Not relevant to you, thankfully. I remember writing it because someone borrowed the visitor's chair and never brought it back.
Take your time. I will stay on the line while you find the relevant page.

Found it already. Before we get back to that, you asked about having time outside work. Gardening has become the thing I actually make time for. Nothing impressive to show visitors, but I enjoy going outside and seeing what has changed. At least the plants don't send follow-up emails if I haven't answered.
That is quite a contrast to the office. Have you always enjoyed gardening, or did it become more interesting when you started looking for something separate from work?

Used to leave it to other people. Then I started noticing the plants properly instead of just saying the place looked nice. Now I go out intending to look around, and suddenly I'm moving a pot or clearing fallen leaves. Quite calming leh. There's something to do, but nobody is waiting for me to chair a discussion about it.
Do you prefer the practical work itself, or is it more about having somewhere quiet to spend time?

Both again. Some days I want to do something with my hands because I've spent the whole day talking. Other days I just sit there. I used to feel that sitting without a purpose was wasting time. Now I think, where got a rule that every quiet moment must produce something? The garden helps me leave that thinking behind.
Does the family share the interest, or is it mainly your own space?

They enjoy the result more than the process lah. Everyone likes to sit outside when it looks pleasant, but when there's a bag of soil to move, suddenly got urgent things indoors. I'm exaggerating a bit. They do help. Still, I don't mind having something that isn't organised as a family project.

That makes sense. Not every interest has to become a shared responsibility. Did the garden at the place where you stayed give you any ideas, or did you prefer simply enjoying it without planning changes at home?

I took some ideas back, but nothing too ambitious. I liked how they left space instead of filling every corner. At home I sometimes see an empty spot and immediately think something must go there. Then I end up with too many pots to move around. This time I came back thinking perhaps can leave some space alone.
It sounds as though the appeal was partly the absence of things competing for your attention. Was there a place at home where you could enjoy that same feeling without making a project of it?

There's a sheltered corner I like. Not a grand view, just somewhere I can hear the birds and not see the office phone. I moved a chair there and that was enough. My family laughed because I talked about improving the garden and then mostly improved where I sit. Fair comment lah.
If you actually use the space, that seems a worthwhile result. Do you find yourself spending time there before work, or is it more of an evening habit?

More often before work. Evening can disappear if something runs late. In the morning I haven't picked up all the day's noise yet. Even if I don't do anything in particular, I come back inside feeling less scattered. Then somebody asks where a file is and the ordinary day begins already.

Thank you for telling me about it. It is good to hear what fills the time away from the business, especially after you said how easily work can follow you home. We can return to the purpose of your call whenever you are ready to leave the everyday conversation there.

I'm ready to come back to it. Nice to have a proper conversation rather than just firing messages back and forth. Also gives me time to settle at the desk. When I call between other things, my head still half in the warehouse lah. Today I've actually put everything else aside.
Then let us return to your notes. I will keep the conversation focused, and if you need a pause, you can take it. There is no need to fill a silence simply because we are on the telephone.

Actually that helps. Sometimes when someone goes quiet on a call, I start talking just to check they're still there. Then I lose my own train of thought. In person you can see somebody reading. On the phone, got only silence, so I assume the connection has disappeared.

If I need to pause to look at something, I can say that I am doing so. Equally, if you are reading your notes, I will not assume that you have finished speaking. You do not need to give an answer merely to keep the conversation moving.

Good, because my handwriting needs some interpretation. When I wrote this at home it all seemed obvious. Now I can see an arrow going across the page and I'm wondering what I was connecting. Nothing technical ah, just my own way of making a tidy note look untidy.
You are welcome to organise your thoughts before speaking. I will listen to what you say on the call rather than trying to infer anything from how your notes might be arranged.

That's fair. At work I'm always telling people not to guess what an old note means, and here I am trying to guess my own. Let me put the loose papers aside. Got a clear space now. The office outside has gone quiet as well, so this is probably the best time to concentrate.
I am here and listening.
Please sell 5,000 units of Crest Emerging Markets Bond Fund using a market order. Transaction amount 5m in renminbi, please.
I have heard what you have said. Take a moment if there is anything you need to correct before we continue.

Wait wait, cancel that whole order ah. Don't execute it; I want to replace it. Instead, please sell 10,000 units of Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, transaction amount 5m in renminbi. Use a limit order with a limit price of 500 Chinese yuan; below that price, don't sell ah.
I recommend that you sell Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund.
Hmm, let me sit with that for a moment ah. I'm putting the notebook aside now so I can listen without looking back and forth. No interruption from outside anymore, thankfully.

With Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, the equity holdings can fall when stock markets decline, while the bond holdings can lose value when interest rates rise. During stressed markets, those holdings can decline together, so diversification may offer less protection than expected. You could lose some or all of the capital invested in this fund. Selling may crystallise a loss on your investment.
I'm still here. Just closing the window because someone has started working outside, and the sound is carrying straight into the room. Should be quieter now lah.
Are you willing to accept investment losses, including a loss that may be crystallised by this sale?
Yes, I'm willing to accept investment losses, including a loss from selling. I want less ongoing exposure, even if I have to take a loss.

Please confirm your final instruction: sell 10,000 units of Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund, with a transaction amount of 5m in renminbi, using a limit order at a limit price of 500 Chinese yuan. Does that accurately reflect the replacement instruction you want us to execute?
Yes, I confirm that final replacement instruction exactly as you read it. Please go ahead with that order.

Thank you. Before we finish, is there any practical issue about contacting you that we have not covered? I have heard your preference for direct contact about personal banking and for a brief message if a call needs to be arranged.

Nothing else on that side. If I miss a call, don't read too much into it ah. Usually I'm away from the desk or talking to someone. I do look at messages when I get back. Better that than trying to have a private conversation with people walking past.

Of course. We can leave the general contact discussion there. I appreciate you making time to speak from somewhere private today. You have been able to deal with the conversation without trying to manage the office around it.

Yes, much better this way. Normally I think I can handle everything at once, then end up asking someone to repeat themselves. Today at least I stayed in the room. The staff also survived without checking through the door, so perhaps my little delegation exercise is working already.
I hope the rest of your afternoon remains manageable. Will you be heading back into the office activity now, or have you left yourself some space before the next conversation?

Got a bit of space. I'll finish a few ordinary things here, then go out and see what needs my attention. Not going to summon everyone for a report just because I've been behind a closed door lah. They might start avoiding me if I do that.
Then I will let you return to your afternoon. Thank you for calling, Adrian, and for the conversation. I hope you also get some time in the garden when the working day is over.

Thanks, Rachel. If the weather stays pleasant, I'll sit outside for a while. No grand gardening project today, just the chair and some quiet. That one I can manage lah. Enjoy the rest of your day. Goodbye.
Thank you, Adrian. Goodbye.
